**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Subject: Religious Studies (code 0785), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Paper 2: The Old Testament/Jewish Bible and World Faiths. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from any ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Sections of the paper: 1.0 The Old Testament/Jewish Bible, Section 1.1 The Patriarchs to David (questions 1 to 6); Section 5.3 Islam (questions 7 to 12); Section 5.5 African Traditional Beliefs and Practices (questions 13 to 18).

questions.enonce_markdown: The visit of the three men to Abraham at the oaks of Mamre is an unforgettable event. Comment. (25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Genesis 18 tells how Abraham, sitting at the door of his tent by the oaks of Mamre in the heat of the day, received three visitors. The narrator says that "the Lord appeared to him", so the story is presented as a meeting with God. It is unforgettable because it joins hospitality, promise, humour and moral concern in a single scene.

**1. Abraham's hospitality.**
- Abraham ran to meet the strangers, bowed to the ground and begged them to stay. He had water brought to wash their feet, rest under the tree, and bread, curds, milk and a tender calf prepared. He stood by them while they ate.
- This reflects the values of the ancient Near East, where welcoming travellers was a sacred duty. The New Testament letter to the Hebrews (chapter 13) later recalls that some "entertained angels without knowing it".

**2. The renewal of the promise of a son.**
- The visitors announced that Sarah would have a son within a year. Abraham and Sarah were very old, and Sarah, listening at the tent door, laughed to herself.
- The reply "Is anything too hard for the Lord?" stresses God's power over human impossibility. The child was later named Isaac, a name linked with laughter. The scene confirms the promise of descendants made in the covenant of Genesis 15 and 17: the covenant would continue through the son born to Sarah.

**3. The disclosure about Sodom and Abraham's intercession.**
- God reveals His plan to examine Sodom and Gomorrah because of the outcry against them. Abraham, as the chosen friend of God, bargains: "Will you sweep away the righteous with the wicked?" and the number of righteous people needed to spare the city is lowered from fifty to ten.
- This shows God as just judge and Abraham as intercessor, a model of bold prayer. Lot's family is later rescued (Genesis 19).

**4. Religious significance.**
- God draws near to humans in ordinary life. Faith is tested and rewarded; hospitality and justice are linked.
- Jews generally read the visitors as God with two angels. Christians have often seen in the story a hint of God's threefold being, and Muslim tradition also remembers Abraham's hospitality to angelic guests. Interpretations differ, but the event is remembered in all three traditions.

**Conclusion.** The visit at Mamre is unforgettable because it shows a generous host, a God who keeps and renews His promise, and a prophet who pleads for others. It confirms that Israel's history rests on God's word, not on human strength.
